A check that asserts an absence records it only beside a control that shows the search works at the scope the claim rests on: the same grep, the same route read or the same census, run against a planted instance, finding it. A search that is misspelled, scoped to the wrong tree or refused by a permission answers zero exactly as a clean tree does, and the zero is then a reading of the search rather than of the code. The planted instance and the real search go in the same output, so a reader who was not there can tell which they are looking at.

A negative control counts as biting only when the run's output **names the assertion it broke**. A bare non-zero exit, an empty output or a `FAIL` line with no failing assertion under it is a run to repeat alone, never a control that bit: a run the pod's memory limit reaped produces exactly that, so a failure-expecting control is satisfied by a run that never happened. Every control mutates a scratch tree and never this issue's workspace, which all six roles share and which `jj` snapshots on any command, so a deliberately broken file left in place reaches the branch at the next commit. A control archives the package under test and every package its test files import, then mutates the copy. Where a control's own words require an edit in place, the control is wrong and comes to the architect to be rewritten, with what it proves unchanged.

# How dispatch://INFRA-1253 is proved

**Who runs what, and where.** This is the owner's rule of 2026-11-16 (dispatch://INFRA-1196/comment/c0b271c7-fd09-485f-8787-862d45795160). No role runs a whole package or a whole suite of tests in the pod, and the tester does not repeat what CI or the implementer already ran.

- **The implementer iterates on one test at a time.** A check written as `go test ./... -run '^Test…$'` is run as `go test <the one package that holds that test> -run '^Test…$'`, with the same flags and the same reads of its PASS and SKIP lines. `./...` in a run string only finds the package.
- **Whole packages and whole suites run in CI.** One `workflow_dispatch` of `ci.yaml` on the issue's branch runs every Go suite and the full browser lane at that head. No role runs them in the pod, to prove a fix or for any other reason.
- **The implementer records each check once, at the head it hands off.** A check that no CI job runs and that takes more than ten minutes, such as a cost check under `-tags basebuild`, runs once at that head.
- **The tester does not run again a check that holds a current result at that head.** It runs the negative control of each check this round changed, which proves that the check can fail. Then it starts Dispatch and drives the workflows this issue changes, through the CLI and the browser as a person and an agent do, with the release before this one running beside this build where the issue changes what two builds share. It records what it saw, and a defect it finds there fails the round.
- **The tester reads before it runs.** For each check the round changed, it reads the test or driver the check names against the check's words. It says whether the test asserts each thing the check states, and whether the test can fail. That reading found every test finding of dispatch://INFRA-1149, and no drive of a check found one (dispatch://INFRA-1196/artifact/retro-model-timeline-md).
- **Each slice is reviewed when it is ready.** The implementer gives each finished slice to a reviewer that has not seen the work, as a subagent, and fixes what it finds before the handoff. One review of dispatch://INFRA-1149 found four critical defects that four test rounds did not.
- **Work that touches different files runs at the same time.** The implementer splits a round's findings by the files they change and runs the groups as parallel subagents, not in one line.

The checks run in a Legion pod, at this issue's own head, in its own pull request. The pod needs these steps once, in order, from the issue's workspace.

```
cd -- "$LEGION_WORKSPACE" && bun install
(cd packages/contracts && bun run build)
export DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL="$LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN" BASELINE_SHA="${BASELINE_SHA:-$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)}"


(cd packages/envoy && go build -ldflags "-X main.buildCommit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -o "$TMPDIR/bin/envoy-dispatch" ./cmd/dispatch) && export PATH="$TMPDIR/bin:$PATH"
psql "$LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN" -c 'create database infra_1253' -c 'create database infra_1253_upgrade'
export INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL="${LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN%/*}/infra_1253"
export INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL="${LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN%/*}/infra_1253_upgrade"
DATABASE_URL="$INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL" DISPATCH_E2E_PORT=8777 bun run dispatch:local > "$TMPDIR/dispatch-local.log" 2>&1 &
until grep -q 'Press Ctrl-C to stop' "$TMPDIR/dispatch-local.log"; do kill -0 $! || break; sleep 2; done
```

`$LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN` is the pod's own test Postgres, never the sessions database that `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` holds. The Go checks read it as `DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, which `storetest.Open` reads and which no other variable replaces: without the export every Postgres test skips in silence, and the check's own proof that its test executed then fails. `storetest.Open` gives each test a new database of its own on that server.    Everything that installs or caches goes under `$TMPDIR`, since the container's own disk is small.

No step exports `DATABASE_URL`. At one worker the browser harness takes a `DATABASE_URL` it finds rather than starting a Postgres of its own, and it truncates and seeds that database, so an exported one would empty a database that other runs in the pod use. This issue has two databases of its own on the pod's test server instead, `infra_1253` and `infra_1253_upgrade`. `INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL` and `INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL` hold their addresses, and no tool reads those names. Each reaches `DATABASE_URL` only as the prefix of a command. What starts a server over either one truncates and reseeds it, so neither is ever the database `$LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN` names.

`infra_1253` is the database of `bun run dispatch:local`, which the last two lines above start on `127.0.0.1:8777`. With `DISPATCH_E2E_PORT` unset the operating system chooses the port, and a run that addresses `127.0.0.1:8777` then finds no server. That command builds and starts this head's server, and it truncates and reseeds its database each time it starts (`packages/dispatch/e2e/local-instance.ts`). It serves the agent bearer `e2e-token` (`packages/dispatch/e2e/run-server.sh`) and seeds the project `CORE` and the person `alice` (`packages/dispatch/e2e/workspace.ts`). It prints `Press Ctrl-C to stop` once it is up, and the last line waits for that. `infra_1253_upgrade` is the database of the drivers that write through the earlier release first, which start their own servers. The build above stamps `main.buildCommit` with this head's commit, as the image build stamps it (`packages/envoy/docker/Dockerfile`), because the conversion's fleet gate compares the commit each live process serves, and an unstamped build serves none. `bun run dispatch:local` builds its own server unstamped (`packages/dispatch/e2e/run-server.sh`), so no driver over `infra_1253` runs the conversion.

Each Go test runs against the pod's test Postgres, which `storetest.Open` reads from `DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` (`packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/store/storetest/storetest.go`). A bare `go test ./... -run <Test>` cannot stand as the gate. It exits zero when the pattern matches nothing, and `storetest.Open` calls `t.Skip` on every Postgres test when that variable is unset. So each Go check runs `-v -count=1`, writes the run's own log under `$TMPDIR`, and then reads that log. It requires the `--- PASS:` line of the test this check states, and it requires no `--- SKIP` line anywhere. A test that is absent, that carries other words, or that skips therefore fails the check rather than passing it. Each Go check below says that in its own body. A driver can also exit zero with a section it needs skipped, or after it stops early, so each driver run requires the driver's closing `PASS: <driver file> complete` line and fails on any `SKIP` line.

Each driver check runs an acceptance driver this issue adds under `packages/dispatch/e2e/acceptance/`, in the shape the five drivers there already take beside `lib.sh`. Its `run` begins `cd packages/dispatch`, because `e2e/acceptance/<file>.sh` is a path from there, and it sets `DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token` and `PROJECT=CORE`. Eight drivers read the `bun run dispatch:local` server above: `c-reparent-and-state`, `c-coverage-states`, `c-issue-relations-read`, `c-duplicate-neighbourhood`, `c-conversation-holds-the-discussion`, `c-tree-read-views`, `c-child-placement` and `c-child-view`. Their `run` also sets `DISPATCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8777` and `DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL`, as `packages/dispatch/README.md` records `DISPATCH_URL`, `DISPATCH_TOKEN` and `PROJECT` for `block-graph.sh`. The other thirteen read rows an earlier release wrote, as the next paragraph requires of every check that converts anything. Each of them starts its own servers, so its `run` sets `DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL` and no `DISPATCH_URL`. A driver that writes as a person sets `DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN=alice` in its `run`. A person's write is a criterion, a comment or a message that must count as a conversation node, an approval, or a Keep of a decision, because a comment or a message an agent wrote is no conversation node, a criterion is a node a person writes, and the Keep route takes a person's credential alone (`routes_table.go`, `model.ScopePerson`). Never run `bun` on these scripts, because Bun's shell cannot run them. Each driver sources `e2e/acceptance/lib.sh`, prints one `PASS` or `FAIL` line per assertion, and exits non-zero on the first failure. It ends with `PASS: <driver file> complete <N> sections`, printed only after its last section, and its `run` greps `^PASS: <driver file> complete `, so a driver that stops early cannot pass.

Every check of this issue that converts anything reads rows an earlier release wrote. A check that reads rows an earlier release wrote is a driver over `infra_1253_upgrade`. A Go check seeds a database that `storetest.Open` migrated to this head. It writes through this head's writers, or by SQL where it needs a row in the shape the release before this one stores, and it says which. A Go test that built an earlier commit would need the `basebuild` tag, which no CI job runs, so the half of a check that needs an earlier build is a shell driver of surface `cli`. Replaying content through this branch's own writer would exercise none of the state the old writer left. That is the fault a second reading found in an earlier draft of this document. So those checks build the earlier release first. This child opens after dispatch://INFRA-1150 merges, as the spec's R6 states and the parent's order fixes, so the commit `BASELINE_SHA` names already carries the deletion of every `decisions.md` and of the `decisions` role, and the earlier release writes three documents for each issue. Each upgrade driver sources `e2e/acceptance/lib-baseline.sh`, which this branch takes as it is from `legion/INFRA-1098` at `f2bdcdfcaae8`, in a commit of its own. At that commit the library stamps each server it builds with its commit, so the base server registers its own commit in `server_processes`. At that commit the library reads `BASELINE_SHA`, boots a prebuilt server named by `BASELINE_BINARY` in place of a build, and passes the `NAME=value` pairs of `BASELINE_EXTRA_ENV`, one per line, to every server it boots. Its `baseline_start` reads the input `BASELINE_SHA`, takes that commit's tree with `git archive` into a directory of its own under `$TMPDIR`, builds `./cmd/dispatch` from it, and boots that build. It adds no `git worktree` and checks nothing out. `BASELINE_SHA` defaults to `git merge-base origin/main HEAD`, as the steps above export it. While a branch this child builds on is unmerged, the implementer sets it to a commit that holds every such branch and none of this child's work, and the handoff names the value. The baseline build carries its own commit, stamped as `lib-baseline.sh` stamps it. The driver stops it before any conversion runs, and a process that stops deletes its own `server_processes` row, so the fleet gate never reads it. Its `run` names `infra_1253_upgrade` as `DATABASE_URL`. Upgrade drivers run one at a time, because each empties `infra_1253_upgrade`. Each server a driver starts serves on a port that `scripts/e2e/lib/held-port.py` chooses and holds, as `lib-baseline.sh`'s `baseline_boot` starts it, so no two servers meet on one port. The driver empties that database first, then calls `baseline_start`, which boots that binary against it. `cmd/dispatch`'s `main` calls `database.Migrate`, so `Store.Migrate` installs the schema of that commit. It never uses `infra_1253`, because `bun run dispatch:local` serves that database and has migrated it to this head. `baseline_boot` starts each of its servers with `DISPATCH_AGENT_TOKEN` set to the `DISPATCH_TOKEN` the run gives, which the server requires (`packages/envoy/cmd/dispatch/AGENTS.md`), and with `DISPATCH_DEV_SIGNIN=1` on loopback, which a person's write through `DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN` needs (`packages/envoy/cmd/dispatch/settings.go`). The driver signs the person `alice` in once through `GET /auth/_dev/signin`. It then creates `PROJECT` there through `POST /api/v1/projects`, with `default_assignee` set to `alice`, because a create by the agent bearer, which acts for no person, must name a person who has signed in (`api/projects.go`). It drives that server's own API to write the fixtures, records what it wrote, and stops it. It then boots this branch's server, the stamped `envoy-dispatch` the preamble puts on `PATH`, over the same database with `baseline_boot`, as the file's own `--selftest` boots it. It boots it with `DISPATCH_TEST_HOOKS=1` and `DISPATCH_TEST_HOLD_ISSUE_ROOM_STEP=1` in `BASELINE_EXTRA_ENV`. That setting holds the conversion step of R6 at boot and on its tick, so this head converts an issue only when the driver runs the command. Production sets neither. Two boots of this head run without that setting: the automatic case of `c-conversion-scope`, and the deferral pass of `c-room-cutover`. That server applies this branch's migrations over those rows. Before it reads anything, the driver waits for the backfill: it polls every 2 s until `select count(*) from document_block_versions where version is null` and the item owed counts (`comment_block_state`, `message_block_state` and `ask_block_state` rows whose `owed_at` is not null) all read 0 and the boot backfill has logged its end, prints each count with the database's `clock_timestamp()`, and fails after 300 s naming the count that stayed above zero. It waits on that condition and never on a fixed sleep. Every row the conversion then reads was written by the earlier release's writers. A driver runs the conversion as `envoy-dispatch convert-issues --project CORE`, the command R6 names. Before it converts, it waits until the newest `server_build_announcements` row names this head's commit, which this head's server writes once every live process serves that commit. It polls every 2 s and fails after 300 s. Each such check says below which rows it captured before the upgrade and compares against that capture.

The fixture the two tree checks seed is one issue carrying all three documents. Those are a spec of two requirement blocks, a Verification document of two check blocks that serve them, and a plan of one task that serves one of those requirements. The issue has three documents and four views, Spec, Verification, Plan and Decisions, because Decisions is a view over decision nodes and not a document. Beside them the fixture holds a conversation written through the real API, which is a comment of two blocks, a message and an open ask. It also holds a criterion a person wrote under the comment's block, and a requirement under that criterion. It holds a comment whose prose cites a block of the Verification document, and a recorded result on one check. It holds one approval of the spec, given before any node moves. It holds one check that serves three requirements under two criteria, which is the shape this document's own checks take. Each conversation block id comes from that item's own blocks read, never from a guess.

`c-old-versions-render`, `c-migration-size` and `c-shared-id-census` each print every count they take, with the time they take it. No check of this tree reads the deployment's rows, because no pod of it can.

## The checks

:::check{#c-tree-census serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-one-tree dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-queries dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-artifacts-in-tree dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-result-node dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-issue-relations dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-document-tree" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE bash e2e/acceptance/issue-tree-graph.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/issue-tree-graph.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: issue-tree-graph.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/issue-tree-graph.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/issue-tree-graph.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="In refs.IndexBlocks, append the part_of tuple of a moved block and skip the document_blocks.parent_block_id update. The census counts one projection row whose parent differs from its tuple, and the driver exits non-zero with that node id, the parent the row holds and the parent the tuple gives."}
This is the issue's census, and it reads zero differences in both directions for every projection this child writes. The driver writes documents through the API covering the shapes the renderer and the block walk disagree on most easily. Those are headings followed by paragraphs, a nested list, and a list whose last item is empty. They are also a typed block that holds a code block, a table, and a quote that holds a list. It then compares each projection with the store, for every issue in `PROJECT`.

The corpus is not only what this branch wrote. Half of it comes from the earlier release, through the base-commit server this document's preamble states. The driver boots that binary and writes the same shapes through its API. It records the block ids, the parents, the ask identities and the citation targets it created, and stops it. It then boots this branch's server, which migrates those rows forward. The driver then waits until `select count(*) from document_block_versions where version is null` and the item owed counts (`comment_block_state`, `message_block_state` and `ask_block_state` rows whose `owed_at` is not null) all read 0. It polls every 2 s, prints each count with the database's `clock_timestamp()`, and fails after 300 s naming the count that stayed above zero. Only then does it take the census. The census runs over both halves, and the driver reports the two halves separately. The driver asserts both halves hold more than zero rows. So a census that reads zero over this branch's rows alone fails here.

The nodes must match. The blocks the server reads back for each document and the block nodes the store holds are equal, id for id. No node is without its row, and no row is without its node. The parents must match. Each node's parent is the node the rendering draws it inside, computed the way `pmdoc.ValidDocument.BlockDescendantIDs` walks it. An authored node is the exception: its parent is its `parent` attribute's target, else its first `serves` target of its own issue, else, for a requirement, the conversation node of its own issue that its `From:` line names first, else the issue. A top-level block of a role document hangs under the issue and never under an artifact; an uploaded document's body hangs under that document's node. The ranks must match. Each node's place among its siblings is the order of its source rows, and two reads of the tree give one order. Siblings compare by rank byte for byte (`collate "C"`). The driver refuses to run, printing a FAIL line, where `select 'a' < 'B'` is false, since such a database cannot tell byte order from its own collation.

It then takes the same two-sided count for five more projections. It takes it for `check_results` against the result nodes and their tuples. It reads each `check_results` row the earlier release wrote, byte for byte as captured before the upgrade, with its check still listing it. It takes it for `issues.parent_key` against the `child_of` tuples and for `issue_links` against the `needs` tuples whose two ends are issues. It takes it for `artifacts` and `artifact_versions` against the artifact, query and document version nodes, and for `node_search` against the text values. It takes it for `components`, `component_depends` and `issue_component_members` against the component nodes and their `part_of`, `depends_on` and `affects` tuples. It prints the count on each side and the symmetric difference for each. It asserts it read more than zero issues, so an empty database cannot pass as equality. It makes no claim about row counts before and after, because a result and an artifact are now nodes and their rows follow the store.
:::

:::check{#c-parent-written serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-one-tree dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-block-parent" surface="cli" run="cd packages/envoy &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; go test ./... -run '^TestTheIssueTreeHoldsTheParentAndRankOfEveryBlockOfTheVersion$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/parent-written.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestTheIssueTreeHoldsTheParentAndRankOfEveryBlockOfTheVersion ' $TMPDIR/parent-written.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/parent-written.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Write the rank only for the ids IndexBlocks collects as changed, and not in reconcileBlockParents. The moved paragraph keeps its first rank, and the test fails with that block id, the rank it kept and the rank the version gives it."}
The run proves this test executed. `go test` exits zero when its pattern matches nothing, so the command reads the run's own log for the `--- PASS:` line of this test. It also fails on any `--- SKIP` line, which is what `storetest.Open` writes when `DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` is unset.

A document is indexed at one version, then at a second that moves a paragraph under a different heading and changes no character of it. `refs.IndexBlocks` writes no `document_blocks` row for such a block, because its text sum equals the stored one (`storedBlocks`), and only `reconcileBlockParents` reaches it. The broken state this case fails on is a rank written only where a row is written. The moved paragraph then keeps its old rank. The test reads the `part_of` tuple of the moved block after the second index. It finds the new holder, with a retraction of the old one at the same time. It reads `document_blocks.parent_block_id` for that block and finds the same holder, and reads the rank values of the moved block and of its new siblings.

The move must cost the block nothing else. The test reads the block's `changed_version` and its `document_block_texts` rows and finds the first version's, because the move changed no text. It reads the Keep recorded on that block before the move and finds it standing, and reads the decision mark on it unchanged. It reads the citation of that block resolving to the same words. A build that bumps `changed_version` for a parent write fails here, with the Keep it cleared.

It then proves the backfill. Documents stored before this work are marked owed, `document_block_versions.version` set null, and the index drains that queue as `docs.Service.RunBlockIndexReconciliation` drains it. Afterwards every block holds the parent and the rank its version's tree gives it. No row is owed, no block id changed, no `block_refs` row moved, and the document's version count is unchanged. Just before the pass, the test reads `select clock_timestamp()` from the database. It finds each tuple's `at` at or after that value and later than the `created_at` of the version the tuple describes. Last it runs an older pass over the same blocks after a newer move. It reads that older pass refused by the fence of dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-write-protocol, with the newer parent still standing.
:::

:::check{#c-conversation-parent serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-conversation-parent dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-from" surface="cli" run="cd packages/envoy &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; go test ./... -run '^(TestAConversationNodeMayBeABlockParent|TestNoAttributeTiesABlockToItsConversation)$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/conversation-parent.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestAConversationNodeMayBeABlockParent ' $TMPDIR/conversation-parent.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestNoAttributeTiesABlockToItsConversation ' $TMPDIR/conversation-parent.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/conversation-parent.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Take the conversation kinds out of the parent attribute's declaration and leave the reference contract widened. The test writes a comment parent, reads the refusal, and fails, because a value the contract reads back is refused on the way in."}
The run proves both tests executed. It greps the run's own log for the `--- PASS:` line of each one by itself. A pattern that matches one test or neither therefore fails the command. It fails on any `--- SKIP` line, which `storetest.Open` writes when `DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` is unset.

`text.FormatItemBlockRef` and `text.CanonicalItemBlockRef` read back exactly what they write for an ask, a comment and a message, and for a block of each. So a parent survives a round trip through markdown with no normalising. A project-document item, a UUID prefix, a non-canonical UUID spelling and a revision pin are each refused.

`pmdoc.ParseBlockPointerValue` and `pmdoc.validateBlockPointerValues` accept those references where a parent is written, and refuse them under an attribute that points at document blocks. So `serves` still points at a block of a document alone, and `needs` points at a plan node and never at a conversation. The shared corpus `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/pmdoc/testdata/block-pointer-values.json` decides every value, which keeps the Go reader and its twin in `@legion/contracts` on one table. `pmdoc.CheckBlockPointers` refuses a conversation of an issue that is neither the writing issue nor one above it, which `refs.IssueAncestors` decides, and refuses a conversation no row holds.

The second test reads the whole schema. It finds no attribute that declares the conversation kinds except the parent, and no attribute called `from`. A planted second attribute declaring the conversation kinds, in a copy of the schema, is found by the same search that finds none in the real one. It then walks up from a block whose parent is the comment's block and reaches the comment and the words in it. It clears that block's stored `parent` attribute value directly in the store, leaving its `part_of` tuple, walks up again and reaches the same comment. So the walk reads the tuple.
:::

:::check{#c-placement-and-coverage serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-serves-coverage dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-reasoning-tree dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-reasoning-tree dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-verification-edges" surface="cli" run="cd packages/envoy &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; go test ./... -run '^TestPlacementAndCoverageAreTwoRelations$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/placement-coverage.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestPlacementAndCoverageAreTwoRelations ' $TMPDIR/placement-coverage.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/placement-coverage.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Derive each check's parent from the first target of its serves pointer on every write rather than on the write that creates it. The retarget case then moves the check under the new requirement, and the test fails, printing the part_of tuple the retarget appended."}
The run proves this test executed. It greps the run's own log for this test's `--- PASS:` line and fails on any `--- SKIP` line, which `storetest.Open` writes when `DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` is unset.

One check serves several requirements and keeps one place. The test seeds two criteria, three requirements under them, and one check whose `serves` points at all three. It reads one check node, one id, one `part_of` tuple and one rank. The parent is the first requirement of the pointer's written order that is a node of the check's own issue, which is what R3 derives at the creating write. It reads three `serves` tuples out of that check.

The broken state the first case fails on is a copy. The test reads the coverage answer and finds the same check under each of the three requirements, with one node id in all three places. It asserts the three entries carry one id and not three. It records one result on that check and reads one result under each of the three entries, counted once in the store. A build that copies the check per requirement fails here, because the three entries carry three ids and the result count is three.

The two changes move apart. The test moves the check under a different requirement through the re-parent route. It reads one appended `part_of` tuple, one retraction, and no `serves` tuple written or retracted. The coverage answer still lists that check under all three requirements it serves. It then retargets the check's `serves` from the first requirement to a fourth. It reads one appended `serves` tuple, one retraction, and no `part_of` tuple written or retracted. The check stays under the parent its move gave it, and the coverage answer drops the first requirement and gains the fourth. The broken state this case fails on is a build that repairs one relation from the other. That shows as a `part_of` tuple written by a retarget, or a `serves` tuple written by a move.

A node whose parent is no longer a requirement it serves reads back with both facts stated. The test reads that node and finds its parent and its three targets, and no read that silently moves it back. It repeats the whole case for a plan node, which carries the same pointer. It then seeds a child issue under the seeded issue, with one check and one plan node whose `serves` names the seeded issue's first requirement alone. Each hangs from the child issue, because it serves no requirement of its own issue, and neither hangs under the parent's requirement. The parent's coverage answer lists each under that requirement through `serves`, marked with the child, and the parent's verification record holds no node of the child. The broken state this case fails on is a writer that takes the first target of any issue. That shows as a `part_of` tuple from the child's check to the parent's requirement. Last it creates two issues, a parent closed as `done` and its child. A child under a `done` ancestor holds requirements of its own (R23). It writes in each a spec that holds the requirement ids this document's `serves` names in `INFRA-1098` and in `INFRA-1253`. It indexes into the child `testdata/infra-1253-verification.md`, a copy of this document committed beside the test, with each `dispatch://TREE-1/` and `dispatch://TREE-2/` reference rewritten to the key of the parent and of the child. It finds `c-tree-census` under each of its six `serves` targets, with one node id, and hanging under `r-one-tree`, the first of its targets that is a node of its own issue.
:::

:::check{#c-criterion-page serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-reasoning-tree dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-conversation-parent dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-serves-coverage dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-reasoning-tree dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-from" surface="api" run="cd packages/envoy &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; go test ./... -run '^TestTheTreeReadAnswersACriterionWithItsAuthorAndItsChain$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/TestTheTreeReadAnswersACriterionWithItsAuthorAndItsChain.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestTheTreeReadAnswersACriterionWithItsAuthorAndItsChain ' $TMPDIR/TestTheTreeReadAnswersACriterionWithItsAuthorAndItsChain.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/TestTheTreeReadAnswersACriterionWithItsAuthorAndItsChain.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Store the person as an author value of the criterion node and append no authored_by tuple. The test fails at the authored_by read, printing the criterion id and no tuple."}
The test creates one issue at this head and writes its spec. No live process announces less than the issue room, so the issue is born converted. It writes, as a person, a conversation on that issue through the API: a comment of two blocks and a message. It also writes an open ask. The test takes each conversation block id from that item's own blocks read.

The test writes a criterion in the issue's room, as a person. The criterion's `parent` value names the first block of the comment. The test reads `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/tree`. The answer holds one criterion node. The node's text equals the text the person wrote, character for character. The node's author is that person.

The test reads the criterion's `authored_by` tuple in the store and finds the same person. It reads the node's attributes and finds no attribute whose value is that person's id or login. It plants such a value in a copy of the node, and the same search finds it. So the empty answer is the node's and not the search's.

The criterion's parent in that answer is the first block of the comment. The test follows the parents the answer gives, starting at the criterion. It reaches the comment and the words in it. The test then reads `?view=spec` from the same route. That answer holds the criterion, marked as the query's. The criterion there carries its parent's id, supertag and first line, which name the first block of the comment.

The test writes a requirement whose `serves` names the criterion. It writes a check and a plan node. Each names that requirement in its `serves`. It records one failing result on the check through `recordCheckResult`. It reads the tree again.

The requirement's parent is the criterion. The check's parent is the requirement. The plan node's parent is the same requirement. The result's parent is the check. So the check is the requirement's child and the plan node's sibling.

The test writes a second criterion and two more requirements. One new requirement names the first criterion in its `serves`, and the other names the second. The test writes one check whose `serves` names all three requirements. It reads the tree again.

The answer holds that check once, with one id, one parent and one rank. The parent is the first requirement in the written order of the pointer. The answer holds three `serves` tuples out of that check, one to each requirement. The test walks the `serves` tuples from each of the three requirements. It reaches that one id each time. So the read answers one node under three requirements and no copy.

The test writes a check whose `serves` points at a block that is not a requirement. It reads the refusal the schema gives for a pointer outside its declared targets. It writes a requirement whose `serves` points at a block that is neither a criterion nor a requirement. It reads the same refusal.

The test reads the rendering of the issue's room. It changes one word of the first requirement in that rendering. It writes the changed rendering to the room and reads the tree again. Every parent and every `serves` tuple reads as before. So the placement survives a round trip through markdown.

The run proves the test executed, because the command reads `--- PASS: TestTheTreeReadAnswersACriterionWithItsAuthorAndItsChain` out of the kept output and fails on any `--- SKIP` line.
:::

:::check{#c-negative-control serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-reasoning-tree" surface="cli" run="cd packages/envoy &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; go test ./... -run '^(TestResultRefusesABeforeMergePassWithNoNegativeControl|TestAClosedIssueRefusesABeforeMergeResultFirst)$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/negative-control.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestResultRefusesABeforeMergePassWithNoNegativeControl ' $TMPDIR/negative-control.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestAClosedIssueRefusesABeforeMergeResultFirst ' $TMPDIR/negative-control.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/negative-control.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Remove the refusal from recordCheckResult. The test reads status 201 for an empty negative control and fails, printing the status it read for a pass that states none."}
The run proves both tests executed. It greps the run's own log for each one's `--- PASS:` line by itself. It fails on any `--- SKIP` line, which `storetest.Open` writes when `DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` is unset.

Recording `verdict: pass` for a `before_merge` check, with an empty `negative_control` in the result's input, is refused `400 NEGATIVE_CONTROL_REQUIRED`, and so is one that is whitespace alone. The error states the field and the check's block id. The same call with a non-empty negative control is recorded, status 201.

A pass on an `after_merge` or `default_branch` check, and a fail on a `before_merge` check, are each recorded with the field empty. A closed issue still answers `409 ISSUE_CLOSED` first, because the new refusal sits after the closed-issue refusal in `recordCheckResult`, which the second test pins. A row stored before this rule, whose `negative_control` is the empty string the column defaults to, still reads back with its verdict, its commit and its role. Its check still lists it, no row is rewritten and no backfill runs.
:::

:::check{#c-one-room serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-one-room" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN=alice bash e2e/acceptance/issue-room.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/issue-room.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: issue-room.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/issue-room.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/issue-room.log &amp;&amp; cd ../envoy &amp;&amp; go test ./... -run '^TestASchemaSwitchClosesEverySocketOfTheIssueRoom$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/schema-switch-room.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestASchemaSwitchClosesEverySocketOfTheIssueRoom ' $TMPDIR/schema-switch-room.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/schema-switch-room.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Key the room on the spec document's artifact id again. The driver opens the issue's room, writes a block that hangs under the comment, and exits non-zero, because the write lands in a room the criterion is not in."}
A person edits one room per issue. On a converted issue, the driver first writes, as `DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN`, a comment and a criterion under it. It opens the document socket for the issue's tree node and writes a block under that criterion. It reads the block back through the issue's tree read, at its place under the criterion, with no second socket opened. It opens the socket for an issue whose tree node it invented and reads the 404 the room check gives.

It proves the server decides the room. The issues this check converts, and the issue it leaves unconverted, were written by the earlier release, through the base-commit server this document's preamble states, so the upgraded database below is one that release wrote. The issue it leaves unconverted is `done`, which the conversion passes over. The driver boots this branch's server over that database, and waits for the backfill as this document's preamble states, and converts the others with `envoy-dispatch convert-issues --project CORE`. It opens the socket for the spec document's own uuid, after that issue converted, and reads the admission to the issue's room. The payload it then writes lands in the issue's tree. It reads the `document_rooms` row for that uuid and finds the issue's tree node as its room. It opens the socket for a document whose issue has not converted and finds that document admitted to itself.

It proves two overlapping views of one issue. It opens two sockets on the issue's room and holds both. One goes through the spec query's old uuid, and one through the Verification query's. It brings both sockets to one state vector. On the first socket it writes one block of the part the second is drawing, and waits until the issue's version count rises by one. Then, on the second socket, it writes one block of the part the first is drawing, from the state vector it held before that first write. Both writes stand afterwards, both views read both, and the issue's version count rose by the writes and no more. The broken state this case fails on is the old one room per artifact. There the second write overwrites the first and one block is gone. The driver asserts both blocks, and prints the one that disappeared when they are not both there.

It proves the three stored tables are untouched by shape. It reads the columns of `doc_updates`, `doc_snapshots` and `doc_checkpoints` out of the catalog of the upgraded database and compares them with the catalog of a database the same migrations build from zero, finding them equal. The comparison is against the migrations as a whole and never against `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/store/migrations/0001_init.up.sql` alone: `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/store/migrations/0041_document_update_classes.up.sql` adds `doc_updates.content_changed`, so the catalog holds five columns where 0001 creates four, on main and on every branch of it, and a check written against the first migration reads an untouched table as a defect. It reads the foreign key of each to `artifacts (id)` and finds it in place.

It then proves what the room admits. A schema version change goes through dispatch://INFRA-1149's schema switch, under that child's R7. The Go test `TestASchemaSwitchClosesEverySocketOfTheIssueRoom` in `internal/dispatch/docs`, written on the pattern of `schema_switch_socket_test.go`, holds a client on the issue's room and changes the installed version. It reads each document socket of that room close, reads the client reconnect to the issue's room at the installed version, and reads no editor of that room left read-only. It reads that outcome for the issue's room rather than for one document. The run proves that test executed, because the command reads its `--- PASS:` line out of the kept output and fails on any `--- SKIP` line.

A node whose parent is in an issue above is read-only in the parent issue's room, and writable in its own. The driver writes that node through the parent issue's room and reads the write refused, naming the node's own issue. It writes it in its own room and reads the new text in both. It reads that node in its own issue's `?view=spec` and in that issue's spec digest, after the nodes the walk from the issue's tree node takes, and it reads the parent issue's digest unchanged by the write.
:::

:::check{#c-room-cutover serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-room-cutover dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-one-room dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-no-regression" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE bash e2e/acceptance/issue-room-cutover.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/issue-room-cutover.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: issue-room-cutover.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/issue-room-cutover.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/issue-room-cutover.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Four controls, run one at a time. First, convert verification-md alone and leave the issue's other two documents in their own rooms. The driver opens the spec and the Verification document, writes one block in each, and exits non-zero, because the two writes land in two rooms of one issue. Second, let an issue be born converted while a live process announces no issue room. The driver reads a document_rooms row for the issue it created beside the baseline server, and exits non-zero naming the issue and that process. Third, make the step and the command convert at once an issue whose document still owes its block index. The driver reads an issue `converted: true` while it still holds the lease, and the conversion's census reads that document's blocks stale. The driver prints the issue and the document and exits non-zero. Fourth, make the step take a deferred issue again only at the next boot. After the driver gives the lease back, both issues stay `converted: false` for 300 s, and the driver exits non-zero naming them."}
Three rooms become one, in one transaction, and no issue is left half converted. The rooms it converts are rooms an earlier release wrote. The driver builds that release the way this document's preamble states and boots it. It edits each of the issue's three documents through that server's sockets. So `doc_updates`, `doc_snapshots` and `doc_checkpoints` hold rows that writer made. It records each room's head state, its row counts and each document's rendered markdown. It stops that server and boots this branch's, which migrates those rows forward, and waits for the backfill as this document's preamble states. The broken state this ordering catches is a conversion that works on rooms its own writer seeded. Such a conversion can lose an update shape the earlier release wrote.

It runs the conversion, `envoy-dispatch convert-issues --project CORE`, and reads the result for that issue. The issue's room holds each of the three documents' content in its own fragment, written in the order R21 states, and the tree's walk shows the spec's blocks first. Each document's text equals the markdown captured before the upgrade, character for character. Its first update was written by the conversion, which the driver reads as the room's version 1.

It proves what the conversion leaves behind. Every `doc_updates`, `doc_snapshots` and `doc_checkpoints` row of the three old rooms is still stored. The driver counts them before the upgrade and after the conversion and finds the two counts equal. The three `document_rooms` rows point at the issue's tree node. The driver then proves the transaction is whole. It creates, in `infra_1253_upgrade`, a trigger on `document_rooms` that raises for the spec artifact id of a second issue the earlier release wrote. It runs the conversion and reads the error naming that trigger. It drops the trigger and finds no `document_rooms` row and no `doc_updates` row keyed by that second issue's tree node.

It proves the reconnecting client. It opens a socket on the spec room and holds it. It runs the conversion. The socket is closed, which `closeRoomOnReplacedHistory` decides, and the driver reconnects with the state vector it held. The reconnection is admitted to the issue's room and reads the converted tree. No write of the held socket reaches a document after the close.

It proves the fleet gate. It boots the baseline build beside this branch's server, stamped with `BASELINE_SHA`, runs the conversion, and reads the refusal naming that build and that instance. It then stops the baseline server. It runs the conversion. The conversion refuses and prints that build and that instance. It removes the row and stops this branch's server, so no process is live. It inserts a `server_build_announcements` row naming another commit, runs the conversion with no server up, and reads the same refusal. It then inserts a row naming the conversion's own stamped commit, and the conversion runs. It boots this branch's server again. The driver reads that the conversion printed each issue it converted, and that a second run over a converted issue changes nothing. It then proves the birth of an issue while only announcing builds are live, two of them of different commits. The second build is this head built again with `main.buildCommit` set to another commit, and the driver boots it beside the first. It creates an issue, writes its spec, and reads a `document_rooms` row to that issue's room from the first write. It stops the second build. A later run passes over that issue without converting it again. A run with `--dry-run` over the same seeded project prints the same issues, each with its time, and a total. After it, every row of `document_rooms`, `doc_updates` and `graph_tuples` reads as it did before, and the real run that follows converts exactly the issues the dry run named. Last, in a second pass over an emptied `infra_1253_upgrade`, the driver keeps the baseline server of `BASELINE_SHA` live and boots this branch's server beside it, as a roll does. It creates an issue through this branch's server and writes its spec. It reads no `document_rooms` row for that issue, and its spec socket is admitted to the spec's own room, as today. It stops the baseline server, runs the conversion, and reads that issue converted. Last, a deferral, in a third pass over an emptied `infra_1253_upgrade`. The driver takes the lease of the block index's reconciliation tick, `docs.BlockIndexLease`, on a `psql` session of its own that it keeps open, with `select pg_try_advisory_lock(1280266064, hashtext('block-index'))`, as `eraseHoldBlockIndex` in `cmd/dispatch/erase_embeddings_test.go` holds it. While it holds that lease, no reconciliation tick runs. A write of 2,000 blocks or fewer still indexes its own blocks in its own request (`deferBlockIndexBlocks`, `docs/reference_excerpts.go`). Through the earlier release the driver writes two issues in flight. The first holds a Verification document of more than 2,000 blocks, which that write leaves to the reconciliation, so that document's `document_block_versions.version` stays null, and the driver reads it null. The second holds documents of a few blocks each. It stops that server and boots this branch's server without `DISPATCH_TEST_HOLD_ISSUE_ROOM_STEP`, and in this pass it does not wait for the backfill as the preamble does, because the owed documents are the case under test. The upgrade marks owed the documents the earlier release stored (R1), and only the reconciliation tick drains them, so while the lease is held both issues owe their block index. While it still holds the lease, it runs `envoy-dispatch convert-issues --project CORE --dry-run` and then `envoy-dispatch convert-issues --project CORE`. Each run prints both issues deferred, each with its reason and a document of that issue that still owes its block index. It accepts any such document of each issue, because the upgrade leaves every document of both issues owed. It reads in the server's log a deferred line of the step for each issue, and it reads both issues `converted: false`. It then gives the lease back and runs no command. It reads `converted: true` for both issues on `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/tree`, every 2 s, and fails after 300 s naming each issue that stayed unconverted. So the step itself converts a deferred issue on a later tick. It reads the conversion's census of each issue at zero.
:::

:::check{#c-reparent-and-state serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-reparent-and-state dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-serves-coverage" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8777 DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN=alice bash e2e/acceptance/issue-tree-reparent.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/issue-tree-reparent.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: issue-tree-reparent.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/issue-tree-reparent.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/issue-tree-reparent.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Two controls, run one at a time. First, append the new part_of tuple and leave the old one standing. The driver reads the subtree under both parents and exits non-zero, with the node id and the two parents it hangs under. Second, let /parent retract the moving node's outbound tuples and append them again with its part_of. The driver reads the second lens's triggered_by tuple retracted and appended again, and exits non-zero naming the lens and that tuple."}
A subtree moves with one appended tuple, and a dead branch stops counting as open. The driver writes, as `DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN`, two criteria. Under the first it writes a requirement with two checks under it. It moves the requirement under the second criterion through the route `POST /api/v1/issues/{key}/nodes/{id}/parent`, with `{id}` the requirement's store address, percent-encoded as one path segment, then reads the tuples. It finds one appended `part_of` to the new parent, one retraction of the old, and no tuple written for either check. It reads the tree and finds both checks under the moved requirement, in the order they had before. It reads each check's `serves` tuples and finds them as they were, so the move changed the place and left the coverage standing.

It reads the refusals. A parent inside the moving subtree is refused, and the error states the cycle. A parent in an issue of another tree is refused, which `refs.IssueAncestors` decides. A move whose stated placement revision is older than the node's current one is refused under dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-write-protocol. The driver reads the newer parent still standing. It reads the rendering before and after the move and finds the moved words unchanged, character for character. It then writes, through dispatch://INFRA-1950's write routes, a lens of kind `pre-mortem` on the first criterion with its `has_kind` tuple, a second lens of kind `pre-mortem` on the second criterion with its `has_kind` tuple and a `triggered_by` tuple to the first lens, and a risk under the first lens with a `prevented_by` tuple to one of the checks. It moves the second lens under the moved requirement through `/parent`. It reads one appended `part_of` tuple and one retraction, and the second lens's `has_kind` and `triggered_by` tuples unchanged. It moves the risk under the second lens, which is of kind `pre-mortem`, through `/parent`. It reads one appended `part_of` tuple and one retraction, and the risk's `prevented_by` tuples unchanged. It then writes a third lens, of kind `trade-off`, and moves the risk under it through `/parent`. The store refuses that move with `400 INVALID_POINTER`, because dispatch://INFRA-1950's store rule lets a risk sit only under a lens of kind `pre-mortem`, and this route holds no copy of that rule. The risk reads back under the second lens, with no tuple appended and none retracted.

It then seeds a third requirement with no check and one plan node under it, and a sibling requirement with no check. It reads both listed as gaps by `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/coverage`, and the plan node with a position in `?view=plan` of the tree read. It sets the third requirement's node `state` to `overtaken` through dispatch://INFRA-1950's route `POST /api/v1/issues/{key}/nodes/{id}/state`, with `{id}` read as in `/parent`. Coverage then lists no gap for it while its sibling's gap stands, and `?view=plan` gives its plan node no position. It reads `select to_id, at from graph_tuples where from_id = <the requirement's node id> and kind = 'state' order by seq` and finds the earlier value with the time it changed, because the value appends. A node `state` value outside the five that dispatch://INFRA-1950 closes the set to is refused `400 INVALID_ATTRIBUTE_VALUE`, naming the attribute and the value it refused. That refusal is dispatch://INFRA-1950's, at the store's attribute write path.
:::

:::check{#c-queries serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-queries dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-result-node dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-verification-edges" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_UPGRADE_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN=alice bash e2e/acceptance/issue-tree-queries.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/issue-tree-queries.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: issue-tree-queries.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/issue-tree-queries.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/issue-tree-queries.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Four controls, run one at a time. First, restore the document lookup in the coverage read, so it finds the requirements through the issue's spec artifact, on an issue whose spec nodes have moved. The read answers no requirement and the driver exits non-zero, printing the empty answer. Second, make the Plan query leave out the `serves` attribute of each plan task. The Plan query then answers a plan task without the `serves` the earlier plan read answered, and the driver prints both and exits non-zero. Third, make the tree read answer the prose blocks of the spec. The driver prints the first prose block it read and exits non-zero. Fourth, make `?view=decisions` answer `waiting_review` true for the decision that is kept. The driver prints that entry with both values and exits non-zero."}
Spec, Verification, Plan and Decisions are the four queries. The issue's relations answer from the same graph and are not a query of their own. The issue this check converts was written by the earlier release, through the base-commit server this document's preamble states, and the driver takes the reads before the move from that issue. It then boots this branch's server, and waits for the backfill as this document's preamble states, and converts the issue with `envoy-dispatch convert-issues --project CORE`. On that converted issue the driver reads `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/coverage` and `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/results`. It compares the fields the earlier release answered, entry for entry and word for word, with what the same reads answered before the move. It finds the same requirements in the same order with the same references. It finds the same checks with their `when`, `surface`, `run` and `negative_control`, the same results, and the same gap lines. The line `<block id> has no plan task` still appears only once the issue has a plan. The driver then compares the four queries and the tree read with the reads they replace, on the same converted issue. The issue holds, written through the earlier release, at least one open ask in its spec and a decision in each review state: one marked replaced, one kept through the Keep route and one waiting review. The driver fails where the earlier decisions read answered no entry in `open_questions`, or no entry in `decisions`, or no decision in one of those three states. Before the move it took, from the earlier release, `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/artifacts/{slug}/text?blocks=true` for the spec, `verification-md` and `plan-md`, and `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/decisions`. Each of the three documents holds prose blocks beside its typed blocks, as a real spec does. Each query is compared over the parts R8 gives it, block by block, keyed by block id, with each block's markdown as the earlier read answered it. The Spec query is compared over the memo callout, where the spec holds one, and the requirement blocks, because no earlier release wrote a criterion. The Verification query is compared over the check blocks, with their `serves`, `surface`, `run`, `when` and `negative_control`. The Plan query is compared over the plan tasks, with their `serves` and `needs`. The tree read with no view answers each of those blocks once, which are the blocks R2 and R16 put in the issue's tree, and it answers no prose block of the three documents, because R2 and R16 keep a role document's prose out of every query. The Decisions query is compared with the earlier decisions read through that read's two members, `open_questions` and `decisions`, entry for entry over the entries the earlier read answered, each keyed by the id that read gives it. For an open question, keyed by its ask id, `?view=decisions` answers the same question and options. For a decision, keyed by its `block_id`, it answers the same heading, text, kind, `replaced`, `kept` and `waiting_review`. `?view=decisions` may also answer entries the earlier read left out, such as an answered ask or an ask outside the spec, so the comparison is not an equality of the two lists. The driver prints every difference with the query and the block or entry it is in.
:::

:::check{#c-coverage-states serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-queries dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-serves-coverage dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-result-node dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-verification-edges" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8777 DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE bash e2e/acceptance/coverage-states.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/coverage-states.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: coverage-states.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/coverage-states.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/coverage-states.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Count any attached result as proof in the coverage read. The driver runs against the `dispatch:local` server of this document's preamble, because it seeds every issue it reads at this head and reads no row an earlier release wrote. `e2e/acceptance/coverage-states.sh` is new here.

The read says what proves a requirement and what does not. The driver seeds four requirements. The first has no check at all. The second has a check with no result. The third has a check whose newest result is a fail. The fourth has a check whose passing result was recorded against a text sum the check no longer holds. The driver makes that fourth case by editing the check after the result. It reads the four back as a gap, as unproven, as unproven, and as unproven. It reads a fifth requirement whose check holds a passing result against its current text, and reads that one proved. The broken state this case fails on is a build that counts any attached result as proof. That shows as the third and fourth requirements reading proved. It then retracts the fifth requirement's passing result through `POST /api/v1/results/{id}/retract`, with a reason. It reads that requirement uncovered, as unproven, because coverage counts a retracted result as no result. It reads the result node unchanged, with the reason as an appended value of its `retracted` attribute, and its `check_results` row unchanged.

The answer comes from the authoritative tuples and from no second cache. The driver retracts one `serves` tuple directly in the store. It reads the coverage answer losing that pairing on the next read, with no index rebuilt and no pass run. It appends the tuple again and reads the pairing back. A build that answers from a second stored copy fails here, because the answer does not follow the tuple.

It then deletes the serving check and reads the requirement uncovered again. It seeds a Verification document of more than two thousand blocks, which the write leaves to reconciliation (`deferBlockIndexBlocks`). A check the block index has not reached has no node, so the driver waits until `document_block_versions.version` of that document is not null. It polls every 2 s and fails after 300 s. It then reads both checks listed in tree order, each with its `serves` tuples. So the deferred index writes the nodes and the tuples that a smaller write writes at once.
:::

It finds the same four under the `Links:` section of `dispatch read --issue`. It creates a second issue with `dispatch issue --duplicate-of`, sets its `filed_from` to the message's canonical reference with `dispatch issue-update --filed-from`, and reads each as a tuple of the store whose target is that issue and that message. On a converted issue `verification_artifact_id` and `plan_artifact_id` each answer the artifact id of their query node, and on an issue that is not converted each answers the id of its role document. The script then searches `packages/dispatch/web/src`, `packages/envoy-client/src` and `packages/daemon` for a reader of either field and finds none, after it finds a planted reader in a scratch copy of one file, so a search that matched nothing cannot read as a clean tree. The driver runs against the `dispatch:local` server of this document's preamble, because it seeds every issue it reads at this head. `e2e/acceptance/duplicate-neighbourhood.sh` is new here.

A component on that server comes from an architecture source on the harness's fake GitHub, as `e2e/acceptance/block-graph.sh` reads one with `COMPONENT_SOURCE=fixture`. No check of this tree passes the port of that fake in its run. `bun run dispatch:local` prints it, as `FAKE_GITHUB_PORT=<port>` in the command it gives for a spec run (`packages/dispatch/e2e/local-instance.ts`), so this run reads it from `$TMPDIR/dispatch-local.log` and gives it as `FAKE_GITHUB_PORT`. The driver seeds the fake, through `PUT /__fixture/repos`, with an architecture repository named for the run that holds one component, K. It adds that repository as an architecture source of `CORE`, syncs it, and removes the source on exit, as `block-graph.sh` does. So no issue that the driver does not seed belongs to K.

It sets every relation through a field of the issue, with two exceptions, each a mention: the body of C holds the literal canonical reference of the ask M, and the spec body of D holds the canonical reference of the issue N. The words of a reference are the words of the key it names, `core` and the issue's number, and, for a reference to an item such as the ask M, the item's path. Each issue's key is among that issue's own words. No text of `CORE` but the body of C holds the reference of M, because H and R reach M through a field. Apart from the words of keys, no text the driver seeds in project `CORE` shares a word with D's text or with another text it seeds there, except the title of G with the title of F.

In project `CORE` it seeds a parent issue P, a blocker issue X, an issue L that holds the ask M, an issue N, and an issue Q. All five are open and in K, and each has a title and a body of its own words. It seeds A, open, in K, under P and blocked by X. It seeds B, `done`, in K and under P. It seeds R, `done`, filed from M through `--filed-from`. It then creates three open issues in this order: C, whose body is the canonical reference of M; H, filed from M; and Y, under N through `--parent`. Each of H, Y and R has a title and a body of its own words. It then writes updates, each a change of priority through `dispatch issue-update --priority`, which changes no word and no target, in this order: H, C and Y, and last P, X, N, Q and L. R gets no update: the driver closes it when it seeds it, so its close is older than the updates of H, C and Y. A and B get no update either, and their places do not depend on the order of the updates: A shares three targets and comes first, and B is the one done issue inside the five. Among C, H and Y, Y holds the newest update, then C, then H, and that order is not the order in which the driver created them. The five issues D links hold the newest updates. It creates a second project through `POST /api/v1/projects`, with `default_assignee` set to `alice`, as this document's preamble creates a project. In that project it seeds E, open, whose body is the canonical reference of M. It then creates D with `dispatch issue`: in K, under P, blocked by X, filed from M and a duplicate of Q, through `--components-json`, `--parent`, `--blocked-by`, `--filed-from` and `--duplicate-of`. D's spec body holds the reference of N and words of its own.

D's output names five neighbours, in this order: A, then Y, C and H, then B. The shared targets of each line are K, P and X for A, N for Y, M for each of C and H, and K and P for B, and the driver compares each line's shared targets with that set, exactly. Y inherits K from its parent N, but R24 counts an issue's own components alone, the ones its `affects` tuples name, so Y's set stays N. So a build that ignores blockers prints A with K and P alone, and a build that ignores a mention on either side, parents, components or filing origins prints a wrong set or a wrong order. Each fails. Open issues come before done ones: a build that orders by the shared count alone puts B second, and a build that leaves done issues out prints four lines. Each fails. Y, C and H share one target each, and the issue with the newer update comes first, so a build that breaks the tie by the time of creation or by the key fails. R, `done`, shares one target, M. It is the sixth candidate, and it is named nowhere, which proves the cap of five. Each line gives the issue's key, its status, its title, the shared targets and a link. No neighbour line names P, X, N, Q or L, which D already links, and the driver reads each one absent. Each of those five is open, shares K with D, and holds a newer update than Y, so a build without the rule of R24 that leaves them out names them after A and ahead of Y, and fails. The output names E nowhere, because E is an issue of another project.

It then seeds F, open, with a title of its own words and no graph target that D shares. It creates G with `dispatch issue --force`, and the title of G repeats the title words of F. `--force` keeps the near-copy gate from refusing G. The driver reads F named in the text lines of G's output, as today's text check names it. So the graph score stands beside the text search, and not in its place. G has no graph target, so the neighbourhood read of G finds no candidate, and the driver reads in G's output the line that says it found none.

It then makes the server's two test hooks hold the neighbourhood read for 15 s and the related search for 4 s, and creates one more issue, T, in K, with `dispatch issue`. This branch adds both hooks under `/_test/`, mounted only under `DISPATCH_TEST_HOOKS`, which `e2e/run-server.sh` sets for the server `bun run dispatch:local` starts. The driver records the time just before it starts the command, and it times the command's wall time. While the command runs, a second process of the driver lists the project's issues through `GET /api/v1/issues?project=CORE` every 100 ms. It finds T within 1 s of the command's start, so the create's write committed before either read ran. The command answers in at most the related search's allowance, 5 s, plus 2 s, which is 7 s. Its output holds the lines of the related search and the line that says the neighbourhood check did not run. A build that runs the two reads one after the other, each under an allowance of its own, takes at least 9 s, and fails. A build that runs them one after the other under one shared allowance answers in 5 s as a correct build does, and this run does not tell it apart. The driver and the server run on one host, so their clocks agree.

Last it runs `dispatch read --issue` on D. Within the `Links:` section it finds `child_of` P, `needs` X, `filed_from` M, `duplicate_of` Q and `affects` K, each exactly once, which proves a `filed_from` to an ask. D's mention of N is not in that section, because D's spec, and not D, holds it. The driver reads that the `Components:` line of the header names K and that the `Node:` line of the read's graph sections names P, as they do today. It counts nothing on those two lines for the rule of once within `Links:`.

The run proves the driver executed, because the command reads its closing `PASS: duplicate-neighbourhood.sh complete` line out of the kept output and fails on any `SKIP` line.
:::

:::check{#c-settlement-reads-back serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-versions-read-back" surface="api" run="cd packages/envoy &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; go test ./internal/dispatch/api/... -run '^TestABrowserEditThatDoesNotReadBackStoresNoVersion$' -count=1 -v 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/TestABrowserEditThatDoesNotReadBackStoresNoVersion.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^--- PASS: TestABrowserEditThatDoesNotReadBackStoresNoVersion ' $TMPDIR/TestABrowserEditThatDoesNotReadBackStoresNoVersion.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q -- '--- SKIP' $TMPDIR/TestABrowserEditThatDoesNotReadBackStoresNoVersion.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Two controls, run one at a time. The test seeds a spec holding a callout inside a list item, and connects a browser peer to its document socket, as `TestABrowserEditCanStoreAVersionThatDispatchCannotRead` of cybermonklabs/legion#4179 does. The peer moves the callout's text into a footnote definition inside the callout and closes its connection. Unless the renderer renders that tree in a form that reads back as the same tree, the artifact then holds no version 2, the log holds the settlement's line naming the room and the parser's error, and the newest version reads back through `pmdoc.ParseRendering`. The peer then moves the text back out of the footnote definition, changes one word of it so the markdown differs from version 1's, and closes again, and the artifact holds a version 2 that reads back and holds that word. Where the renderer does render that tree readably, the test reads version 2 stored and reading back as the edited tree instead.

The test then writes, straight into `artifact_versions`, a newest spec version of a second issue that the parser refuses, and runs the conversion. The conversion passes over that issue with the parser's error in its log line and converts the other issue. The run proves this test executed: it greps the run's own log for this test's `--- PASS:` line and fails on any `--- SKIP` line.
:::

:::check{#c-conversation-holds-the-discussion serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-queries dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-document-tree" surface="cli" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8777 DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN=alice bash e2e/acceptance/conversation-view.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/conversation-view.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: conversation-view.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/conversation-view.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/conversation-view.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Three controls, run one at a time. The conversation view answers the discussion and nothing else. The driver seeds one issue carrying every node kind this model holds: a thread of comments with replies that a person wrote as `DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN`, an ask with its answer, a remark nobody answered, a criterion the person wrote in that exchange, a requirement under that criterion, a decision an agent recorded with its `shaped` tuple to the requirement, a check and a plan task that serve it, a person's approval of the spec, two documents with several versions each, and a child issue. It reads the conversation graph and asserts by kind that it answers the comments, the asks with each answer held on its ask, the replies, the remark, the criterion, the requirement, the decision, the check and the plan task, because a requirement, a decision, a criterion and an element of the plan are revealed by going down the discussion and are nodes of that graph. It also seeds a message the Legion daemon's own session posts on the issue, and asserts that the conversation graph does not answer it, while the issue's messages still hold it. It seeds an agent's status comment at the top of the issue and an agent's reply inside a thread a person started, and asserts the tree leaves out the first and answers the second, while the issue's comments hold both. It seeds the spec's Summary paragraph as a prose block of the spec document, and asserts the tree does not answer it, while its document version still renders it. It seeds the spec's first callout as its three-thing memo. It asserts the tree answers that `callout` node first, that `?view=spec` answers it first as a node of the query, and that a change to one of its three sentences moves the digest the spec approval records. The seed also holds a second callout, which is not the issue's first child. `?view=spec` does not answer that callout, and an edit of it moves no spec digest. A third issue's first child is a paragraph, and the issue holds a callout after it. Its `?view=spec` answers no callout at all. It makes every read of the tree through `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/tree`. It also seeds a second issue with as many blocks, comments, asks and messages as the largest of the ten issues R8 measures. The pull request body records those counts, and the driver holds them as constants. It reads that issue's whole tree in one request, and prints the page size and the node count beside it. It gives the seeded child issue an ask, and reads that ask in the child's tree, as a conversation node of that child. An answer is no kind of its own, because dispatch://INFRA-1098 R21 holds it as attribute tuples of its ask. It asserts that the conversation answers no artifact, no document version and no prose block of a role document, all of which are nodes of the issue and are reachable from it, so the assertion can fail and does when any is let in. It asserts nothing about a claim, a handoff or a status move, because this model has no such node kind for one to appear as: a check that forbids what cannot exist proves nothing. A node the tree must leave out, if it is in the answer, is printed with its kind and its id, and the driver fails. It asserts in the same read that a remark nobody answered, which produced no requirement and no decision, is present as a node of its own, since plain prose is a node and a view that drops it has made the discussion tidier than it was.
:::

:::check{#c-tree-read-views serves="dispatch://TREE-2/spec#b-r-queries dispatch://TREE-1/spec#b-r-document-tree" surface="api" run="cd packages/dispatch &amp;&amp; set -o pipefail &amp;&amp; DATABASE_URL=$INFRA_1253_DATABASE_URL DISPATCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8777 DISPATCH_TOKEN=e2e-token PROJECT=CORE DEV_SIGNIN_LOGIN=alice bash e2e/acceptance/tree-read-views.sh 2&gt;&amp;1 | tee $TMPDIR/tree-read-views.log &amp;&amp; grep -q '^PASS: tree-read-views.sh complete ' $TMPDIR/tree-read-views.log &amp;&amp; ! grep -q '^SKIP' $TMPDIR/tree-read-views.log" when="before_merge" negative_control="Eleven controls, run one at a time.
